main.title: Metal Slug 2
main.subtitle: The squad grows
main.summary: Metal Slug 2 is SNK's run-and-gun sequel, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 23 February 1998.

cards.heading: The squad grows
cards.text: Metal Slug 2 is SNK's run-and-gun sequel, first released for Neo Geo MVS in Japan on 23 February 1998. Marco and Tarma return alongside Eri and Fio as General Morden's forces begin another campaign. One or two players move through densely animated stages, shooting enemies, collecting weapons and taking control of vehicles before confronting a large boss. The expanded squad accompanies a wider range of settings and transformations, carrying the original's comic military action towards a stranger conflict involving creatures and machines from beyond its familiar army.

cards.heading: A rescue worth protecting
cards.text: Prisoners rescued along the route provide weapons or other useful items. Reaching the end of a mission preserves them for a score bonus, while losing a life clears the current rescue tally. A successful run therefore means protecting progress as well as collecting it. Destructible scenery can conceal further supplies, encouraging shots beyond the obvious enemy targets. Tanks add weapons and protection, while close-range knife attacks handle opponents within reach. The player repeatedly moves between vulnerable infantry fighting and brief opportunities to command something much more powerful.

cards.heading: The battlefield becomes stranger
cards.text: Transformations alter the soldier's abilities during certain sections, making an unexpected condition part of handling the next obstacle. Helpers also appear: the rescued Hyakutaro can fight alongside the squad, while Rumi supplies additional items. These small encounters reinforce the animation's humour while providing practical assistance. Takushi Hiyamuta composed the music, continuing the series' energetic accompaniment. The original release also suffered substantial slowdown in busy scenes, leading to the later reworking Metal Slug X. The sequel established the larger cast and increasingly fantastical action that subsequent games would continue to expand.

main.title: Burning Rangers
main.summary: Sonic Team's futuristic rescue game combines firefighting, jet-assisted movement and spoken directions through dangerous buildings.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Burning Rangers is a third-person action game developed by Sonic Team for Sega Saturn and released in 1998. Playing as rookie rescuer Shou or Tillis, the player joins a futuristic firefighting squad, using an energy weapon and a jet-equipped suit to reach people trapped inside hazardous facilities.

cards.heading: Every crystal can save someone
cards.text: Extinguished flames leave crystals behind, and collecting them makes rescue possible: five crystals are needed to teleport a survivor to safety. The same supply also protects the Ranger from damage, so every rescue uses part of the player's safety net. Floors and walls can erupt as the danger level rises. Clearing a route means watching the surroundings as well as aiming at the fire directly ahead, then gathering enough crystals to help the next person found inside.

cards.heading: Follow the voice
cards.text: Directions arrive through the team's radio. The controller guides the Ranger towards a corridor, a door or a change of level, and the player can ask to hear the instruction again. Listening becomes part of finding the way through these multi-storey spaces. Jet-assisted jumps carry the Ranger across gaps and up towards ledges; underwater passages change the movement again. The crackle of fire, warning sounds and voices give a room information that its walls alone cannot provide.

cards.heading: A rescue worth returning to
cards.text: A completed mission leaves a record of the rescue: its rank reflects how effectively the emergency was handled. Finding more survivors gives a reason to return to places that initially demanded a hurried escape. After the main game, a route generator changes the arrangement of passages for another run through the facilities. The settings range from industrial interiors to underwater and orbital locations, keeping the same task at the centre of the spectacle: reach the people inside, then get them out.

main.title: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins
main.subtitle: A ninja succeeds by remaining unseen
main.summary: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins is Acquire's PlayStation stealth game, first released in Japan on 26 February 1998. Rikimaru and Ayame undertake missions for Lord Gohda in a fictionalised Sengoku-era Japan. The player chooses a ninja, prepares equipment and enters a place where observing guards matters more than winning a public fight. Rooftops and concealed approaches provide room to plan. The game makes the ninja's familiar tools into practical ways of moving through three-dimensional space, asking the player to arrange an encounter before the enemy knows that an encounter has begun.

cards.heading: A ninja succeeds by remaining unseen
cards.text: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins is Acquire's PlayStation stealth game, first released in Japan on 26 February 1998. Rikimaru and Ayame undertake missions for Lord Gohda in a fictionalised Sengoku-era Japan. The player chooses a ninja, prepares equipment and enters a place where observing guards matters more than winning a public fight. Rooftops and concealed approaches provide room to plan. The game makes the ninja's familiar tools into practical ways of moving through three-dimensional space, asking the player to arrange an encounter before the enemy knows that an encounter has begun.

cards.heading: Look before dropping from the roof
cards.text: The grappling hook gives access to high positions from which patrols and possible routes can be studied. Other tools can distract, delay or harm a guard, but only a limited selection can be carried into a mission. Rikimaru and Ayame differ in speed and fighting style, changing how an exposed situation feels. Remaining unseen creates opportunities for quiet attacks; being discovered forces a less comfortable response. Each successful approach begins with reading the space, then choosing when to move from safety into the guard's reach.

cards.heading: Stealth finds another three-dimensional form
cards.text: Acquire began production in 1996 with a small team, and director Takuma Endo took on several roles, including scenario writing. Noriyuki Asakura's music supported a setting unusual among the period's modern military stealth games. Activision published the Western editions later in 1998, bringing the game to a wider audience. Its reception and sales led to Tenchu 2 in 2000. The original's lasting image is an ordinary stretch of roof above an unsuspecting guard: a simple arrangement that gives the player time to watch, choose and act.

main.title: Bushido Blade 2
main.subtitle: A duel can end before it settles into a rhythm
main.summary: Bushido Blade 2 is Lightweight's PlayStation weapon-fighting game, first released in Japan on 12 March 1998. Rival schools of assassins pursue their own goals through confrontations where a well-placed strike can decide the outcome abruptly. The player chooses a fighter and weapon, then judges distance, stance and the opponent's movement instead of simply wearing down a long health bar. The sequel gives the Narukagami and Shainto schools a more structured conflict, keeping the original's interest in the danger carried by a single blade while rearranging the journey around it.

cards.heading: A duel can end before it settles into a rhythm
cards.text: Bushido Blade 2 is Lightweight's PlayStation weapon-fighting game, first released in Japan on 12 March 1998. Rival schools of assassins pursue their own goals through confrontations where a well-placed strike can decide the outcome abruptly. The player chooses a fighter and weapon, then judges distance, stance and the opponent's movement instead of simply wearing down a long health bar. The sequel gives the Narukagami and Shainto schools a more structured conflict, keeping the original's interest in the danger carried by a single blade while rearranging the journey around it.

cards.heading: Read the weapon before entering its reach
cards.text: Swords and polearms give the fighters different possibilities at close and middle distance. Moving forward is a commitment because an opponent can answer before a combination has properly begun. The sequel adds dual-sword attacks and changes several of the first game's systems, asking returning players to adjust familiar habits. Support characters appear during the story, and completing a stage with one can unlock that fighter elsewhere. The roster therefore grows through participation in the campaign, making another encounter an opportunity to learn a different relationship between reach, movement and risk.

cards.heading: From one connected place to successive skirmishes
cards.text: The original's large connected setting gives way to a sequence of maps, often placing groups of lesser opponents before a rival from the other school. This creates a more clearly staged progression while retaining the threat of decisive weapon contact. Kunihiko Nakata directed the sequel, with Ryuji Sasai composing its music. The North American release followed in October 1998. Bushido Blade 2 remains unusual among its contemporaries because the exchange is always fragile: the player has to respect the next attack even before a long contest has had time to develop.

main.title: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit
main.summary: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit is a 1998 racing video game developed for PlayStation by EA Canada and Microsoft Windows by EA Seattle, and published by Electronic Arts.

cards.heading: Police pursuits join the race
cards.text: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit is a 1998 racing video game developed for PlayStation by EA Canada and Microsoft Windows by EA Seattle, and published by Electronic Arts. It is the third major installment in the Need for Speed franchise, incorporating police pursuits as a major part of gameplay. Hot Pursuit remains focused on racing using exotic sports cars, but features races that primarily take place in locations within North America, including varied settings and climates. Police AI is improved over the first game, utilizing several tactics to stop both the player and opponent.

cards.heading: PlayStation, Windows and later successors
cards.text: The PlayStation version was released on March 25, 1998, while the Windows version was released on September 23, the same year. The game received critical success, with praise for its graphics and customization options. It received a direct sequel in 2002 and a reboot in 2010.

main.title: Tail Concerto
main.subtitle: A policeman among floating islands
main.summary: Tail Concerto is CyberConnect's first game, an action-adventure released for PlayStation in Japan on 16 April 1998. Waffle Ryebread, a young canine policeman, pilots a Police Robo through the floating islands of Prairie. His encounters with the Black Cats Gang connect small disturbances to a search for dangerous crystals. Airships, steam machinery and ancient ruins give the world its setting, while dogs and cats supply its inhabitants. Nobuteru Yūki's character designs help the machines and expressive animal cast belong to the same light-hearted adventure, even as their disagreements reveal deeper tensions.

cards.heading: A policeman among floating islands
cards.text: Tail Concerto is CyberConnect's first game, an action-adventure released for PlayStation in Japan on 16 April 1998. Waffle Ryebread, a young canine policeman, pilots a Police Robo through the floating islands of Prairie. His encounters with the Black Cats Gang connect small disturbances to a search for dangerous crystals. Airships, steam machinery and ancient ruins give the world its setting, while dogs and cats supply its inhabitants. Nobuteru Yūki's character designs help the machines and expressive animal cast belong to the same light-hearted adventure, even as their disagreements reveal deeper tensions.

cards.heading: Arms made for catching
cards.text: The Police Robo runs, jumps, climbs ledges and briefly hovers. Its mechanical arms lift and throw objects, while a bubble blaster immobilises enemies at a distance. Capturing troublesome kittens therefore involves getting close enough to grab them, not simply firing until they disappear. Objectives change between stages, with mine carts, a jet pack and guided missiles supplying other ways to travel or fight. The large machine becomes an adaptable body for Waffle: each tool changes how he crosses a place and what he can do when he reaches its inhabitants.

cards.heading: Small discoveries between duties
cards.text: Towns allow Waffle to talk with residents between the action stages. Hidden whistles grant extra lives, and boxes contain fragments of pictures that become viewable in a gallery when assembled. These discoveries give corners of the islands another purpose beyond the current police assignment. Chikayo Fukuda and Seizo Nakata composed the music; the Japanese opening uses Kokia's For Little Tail. A French release followed in 1998 and an English North American edition in 1999. Despite an encouraging critical response, Japanese sales fell short of expectations, leaving the setting as a smaller, distinctive PlayStation adventure.

main.title: Baroque
main.summary: Baroque is a roguelike role-playing video game developed by Sting Entertainment.

cards.text: Baroque is a roguelike role-playing video game developed by Sting Entertainment. It was originally released for the Sega Saturn in 1998 by Entertainment Software Publishing, then ported to the PlayStation the following year. A remake for PlayStation 2 and Wii was released in Japan by Sting Entertainment in 2007, and later overseas in 2008 from Atlus USA (North America) and Rising Star Games (Europe). This version was later released on iOS in 2012, and an enhanced port of the original version on Nintendo Switch in 2020.

Baroque is set in a post-apocalyptic world where an experiment to understand the Absolute God caused devastating climate change, with surviving humans becoming physically twisted by manifestations of guilt. This experiment was led by a being called Archangel. The protagonist is guided by Archangel through the Neuro Tower to find the Absolute God and fix the world. All versions of the game feature dungeon-crawling through randomly-generated floors of the Neuro Tower, with deaths in the dungeon advancing the narrative. The original uses a first-person perspective, while the remake includes a third-person camera and adjustable difficulty levels.

The game was conceived by Kazunari Yonemitsu, who was involved in multiple aspects of its design and created the narrative. Originally in production for the PC-9800 series, Yonemitsu's wish for 3D graphics resulted in it shifting to the Saturn. Its dark tone, a reaction to Yonemitsu's previous work, was influenced by European cinema and film noir. The gameplay drew inspiration from Torneko no Daibōken: Fushigi no Dungeon. The music was composed by Masaharu Iwata, who blended ambient noise and sound samples into the tracks. Baroque was supported with several supplementary products, including a visual novel based on a promotional novella. The remake featured new staff and several changes, including redone character designs from Kenjiro Suzuki and replacement music by in-house composer Shigeki Hayashi. The game saw generally mixed reviews from critics.

main.title: Unreal
main.summary: Unreal is a 1998 first-person shooter game developed by Epic MegaGames and Digital Extremes and published by GT Interactive for Microsoft Windows.

cards.heading: A prisoner escapes onto an alien planet
cards.text: Unreal is a 1998 first-person shooter game developed by Epic MegaGames and Digital Extremes and published by GT Interactive for Microsoft Windows. Set in a science-fiction universe, the player controls a prisoner whose prison spacecraft crash-lands on a mysterious planet, where they must find a way to escape while combatting the occupying alien empire. It is the first entry in the Unreal game series and was powered by the titular Unreal Engine. The game reached sales of 1.5 million units by 2002.

cards.heading: Na Pali, Unreal Gold and later releases
cards.text: Since the release of Unreal, the franchise has had many entries including one sequel and a spin-off series with multiple commercially successful and award winning games based on the Unreal universe referred to as the Unreal Tournament series. One official bonus pack, the Epic-released Fusion Map Pack, can be downloaded free of charge. Unreal Mission Pack I: Return to Na Pali, developed by Legend Entertainment, was released in June 1999, and added 17 new missions to the single-player campaign of Unreal. Unreal and Return to Na Pali would later be bundled together with the updated version of the game's engine from Unreal Tournament and released as Unreal Gold. In 2024, the game officially became freeware with Epic Games’ blessing.

main.title: Radiant Silvergun
main.summary: Radiant Silvergun is a shoot 'em up video game developed and published by Treasure.

cards.heading: Six shots, a sword and tightly designed stages
cards.text: Radiant Silvergun is a shoot 'em up video game developed and published by Treasure. It was originally released in Japanese arcades in 1998 and subsequently ported to the Sega Saturn later that year. The story follows a team of fighter pilots in the far future who are battling waves of enemies summoned by a mysterious crystal dug up from the Earth. The player has an arsenal of six different types of shots to choose from, and a sword to destroy nearby targets. The stages are tightly designed to present players with scenarios that can be approached differently with the various weapon types.

cards.heading: A small team takes an arcade risk
cards.text: Treasure was primarily known for developing action and platform games for home consoles before Radiant Silvergun. Despite the company's concerns about the financial viability of arcade games and the shooter genre, they felt they had a good premise for a game and decided to pursue it. Radiant Silvergun was developed by ten people, with Gonzo outsourced for animated cutscenes. The game was developed for the ST-V arcade board first and later ported to the architecturally similar Sega Saturn. Towards the end of development, the team recruited professional gamers that held high scores in shooters to play test the game.

cards.heading: From a Japanese release to worldwide ports
cards.text: Radiant Silvergun was first released in Japanese arcades in May 1998. Treasure president Masato Maegawa went in person to arcades to gauge the reaction of players. The Saturn port was released two months later in Japan. Despite its region exclusivity, Radiant Silvergun was imported by Western critics and received critical acclaim. Journalists agreed that the game revived the shoot 'em up genre, which had fallen by the wayside after the rise in popularity of arcade fighting games in the 1990s. In retrospect, it is considered one of the greatest shooters and Sega Saturn games of all time. It received a spiritual sequel in the form of Ikaruga (2001), and was ported worldwide to the Xbox 360 in 2011, to the Nintendo Switch in 2022 and to Windows in 2023.

main.title: Devil Dice
main.subtitle: Turning the floor into a puzzle
main.summary: Devil Dice is Shift's PlayStation puzzle game, first released in Japan as XI on 18 June 1998. A small devil runs across a field of oversized dice, climbing on top to roll them into useful positions. Matching numbers makes groups sink and disappear, but reaching the correct face requires thinking about how each die will turn along the way. The board is both a moving platform and the material of the puzzle. That connection lets a simple-looking field produce increasingly difficult decisions about position, orientation and the space available for the next move.

cards.heading: Turning the floor into a puzzle
cards.text: Devil Dice is Shift's PlayStation puzzle game, first released in Japan as XI on 18 June 1998. A small devil runs across a field of oversized dice, climbing on top to roll them into useful positions. Matching numbers makes groups sink and disappear, but reaching the correct face requires thinking about how each die will turn along the way. The board is both a moving platform and the material of the puzzle. That connection lets a simple-looking field produce increasingly difficult decisions about position, orientation and the space available for the next move.

cards.heading: A six needs six neighbours
cards.text: A group must contain at least as many matching dice as the number showing on their upper faces. Two twos can begin a clear, while sixes require a larger gathering. The dice sink gradually, leaving a short opportunity to add more matching pieces and extend the chain. Running in a direction rolls the die beneath the devil, exposing another face and changing where he stands. The useful move therefore has two consequences at once: it prepares a number and carries the player towards, or away from, the next part of the arrangement.

cards.heading: From an open call to the living room
cards.text: Devil Dice emerged from Sony's Game Yarōze initiative, which invited proposals that could become commercial PlayStation games. Lead designer Yuichi Sugiyama and programmer Shuichi Yano later described that route into development, distinguishing it from the similarly named Net Yaroze programme. The finished game combined solitary puzzle solving with competitive modes, including play for five people through a multitap. Critics welcomed the idea while noting its difficulty. Kemmei Adachi composed the music, and later related games carried the rolling-dice concept to other hardware, including the PlayStation 2 follow-up Bombastic.
